muc.title: Holding a hammer, everything looks like a nail
muc.text: With AI in hand, you want to give it every task. It's like holding a hammer: everything looks like a nail. But not every task is worth it.

muc.title: Two filter questions
muc.text: Before you start, ask two questions. One: if AI gets it wrong once, what happens? Two: is it easy to check its work?

muc.title: AI's sweet spot
muc.text: Drafting an email, summing up a meeting, naming a new cake. If it's wrong, you fix a few words, and one glance tells you if it's right. This is AI's sweet spot.

muc.title: The red zone: AI helps, people decide
muc.text: But calculating salaries, diagnosing illness, signing contracts for you: one mistake costs money or health, and checking it almost means redoing it from scratch. Here, AI should only help, and a person must decide.

muc.title: When a formula is enough
muc.text: Some tasks don't need AI at all. Calculating tax with a fixed formula? A spreadsheet is enough: faster, cheaper and right every time.

muc.title: Put it all in one table
muc.text: Put it all in one table: small mistakes that are easy to check, do it now. Big mistakes that are hard to check, avoid. In between, let AI draft and a person approve.

muc.title: Score your own tasks
muc.text: Write down three tasks you do each week, and score each with those two questions. Hand the ones in the "do it now" box to AI first.

muc.title: AI still makes mistakes sometimes
muc.text: You've picked the right tasks. But AI still gets things wrong sometimes. How do you design so those mistakes don't cause harm? See you in part 3.
